note: greek religion kept animist elements beside its pantheon of gods
why: Page says Greek and other pagan religions had animist roots and kept them alongside pantheons; no spirits-to-gods sequence stated.

note: bach reads aristotle's soul, the form animating a body, as animist
why: Bach and Sorensen's essay says Aristotelianism may be understood as animist; no source shows Aristotle building on prehistoric animism.

note: a disputed Pythagorean influence on Plato's metaphysics and mathematics
why: SEP 3.7: wide disagreement; influence on Plato's late theory of principles and mathematical cosmology, but narrower than often assumed.

note: the stoics made logos the rational order of the cosmos
why: Stoics held their tenets derived from Heraclitus, especially the logos, as rational law governing the universe.

note: descartes set out to prove the soul immaterial, as the church asked of christian philosophers
why: SEP: Descartes cites the Lateran Council's injunction to prove the soul's immateriality; Christian thinkers had adopted Platonic dualism.

note: la mettrie extends descartes' animal-machine to humans and drops the soul
why: Page says La Mettrie extends Descartes' animal-automaton argument to humans and denies a soul separate from matter.

note: the rationalist side kant tries to reconcile
why: SEP gives the conventional view: Kant steering between Leibnizian-Wolffian rationalism and Hume's empiricism.

note: ethics as calculation
why: SEP: Bentham consciously allied himself with the Enlightenment and its thinkers; describes his felicific calculus of pains and pleasures.

note: cells as agents that cooperate to build bodies
why: Levin's 2019 paper does not mention cell theory; no source found tying his cell-agency work to it.

note: the ignorabimus is seen as anticipating mysterianism, though the two views differ
why: One paper says it anticipates McGinn's mysterianism; another says they cannot be assimilated and McGinn's own sources were Huxley and Locke.

note: psychology becomes a laboratory science
why: Page discusses James's 1874 demonstration laboratory and Wundt's 1879 Leipzig research laboratory together as psychology's first labs.

note: watson's behaviorism rejected introspective methods; skinner's later treated introspection as behaviour
why: Pages: Watson rejected introspection for observable behaviour; Skinner's radical behaviorism accepts introspection as behaviour; Wundt brought introspection into experimental psychology.

note: logic as the form of language
why: SEP: the Tractatus evolved as a continuation of and reaction to Russell and Frege's conceptions of logic and language.

note: frege's semantics for his formal language anticipates tarski's theory of truth
why: Both papers call Frege's semantic theory similar to Tarski's truth theories, Frege the 'grandfather'; neither says Tarski drew on it.

note: lisp and scheme
why: SICP itself says Lisp's lambda notation is adopted from Church's lambda calculus.

note: the stored-program computer
why: Page quotes Frankel: von Neumann firmly emphasised that the fundamental conception of the stored-program computer is owing to Turing.

note: 'can machines think?'
why: Stanford history: Turing's 1950 essay explored many ingredients of AI before the 1956 Dartmouth workshop named the field.

note: information and compression as a theory of induction
why: Solomonoff writes that Shannon's papers had a profound effect on his ideas about induction, linking information and probability.

note: schmidhuber generalises solomonoff's algorithmic probability and universal prediction
why: Schmidhuber's page presents generalised Kolmogorov complexity with consequences for Solomonoff's theory; it does not phrase this as learning as compression.

note: prediction and compression
why: Bell, Witten and Cleary ground text compression in Shannon's source coding theorem and his prediction experiments on English.

note: reliable computing from unreliable parts
why: Ackley cites von Neumann's 1948 prediction of computing in which all operations tolerate faults, and argues for it.

note: wolfram cites life as a universal 2d cellular automaton, but calls it recreation, not science
why: Wolfram's 1982 paper cites Life as an example; his history note says almost no systematic science came from it.

note: the universe as a cellular automaton
why: Zuse proposed the universe is computed on a cellular automaton and cited von Neumann's book on self-reproducing automata.

note: overlapping but distinct: a computational universe need not be one run by someone
why: Page says digital physics overlaps with but is distinct from the simulation hypothesis; it does not say one implies the other.

note: information as more basic than matter
why: Page gives Wheeler's 'it from bit' as the slogan for informational primacy, one strand of digital physics.

note: unlimited complexity from a tiny rule
why: Textbook chapter treats the Mandelbrot set and Conway's Life together as simple rules producing complex behaviour.

note: neural nets, then minsky's critique of them
why: Page: Minsky was inspired by McCulloch and Pitts, built the SNARC neural net, then co-wrote Perceptrons on their limits.

note: second-order cybernetics
why: Page lists Maturana and Varela's autopoiesis among the theories developed within second-order cybernetics.

note: what keeps a living system ordered
why: Page says autopoiesis, autocatalytic sets and related theories found their original inspiration in Schrödinger's What Is Life?

note: pattern matching that feels like understanding
why: Pages call ELIZA a symbolic AI chatbot whose pattern matching gave users an illusion of understanding.

note: a crowd of demons becomes a society of mind
why: Johnson: Selfridge's demons are what Minsky's Society of Mind calls agents; Museum of AI says it drew on Pandemonium; Minsky called Selfridge a mentor.

note: the transformer
why: Page says LLMs are typically based on the transformer neural network architecture.

note: skill is not intelligence
why: Chollet argues skill at tasks is not intelligence, and criticises the deep-learning era's tabula-rasa framing and benchmark shortcuts.

note: the neural ca paper names life as the classic cellular automaton before its learned ones
why: Paper mentions Conway's Life as what popularised cellular automata; it does not say its method derives from Life.

note: dreyfus's heidegger-based critique of symbolic ai is among those embodied cognition takes up
why: IEP lists Dreyfus among problems raised for cognitivism that embodied theorists share; no page says the field builds on him.

note: runaway self-improvement
why: Page links the intelligence explosion to existential risk, Bostrom's extinction scenarios and Yudkowsky's MIRI.

note: man a machine
why: Materialism page places La Mettrie among the French materialists; Man a Machine is described as a work of materialist philosophy.

note: functionalism is neutral on substance but attractive to materialists, as an alternative to identity theory
why: SEP: functionalism is officially neutral between materialism and dualism, though especially attractive to materialists.

note: turing's work inspired putnam's machine-state functionalism
why: SEP: Turing's work was the avowed inspiration for Putnam's machine-state theories; multiple realisability is not derived from universal computation.

note: 'troubles with functionalism'
why: SEP presents Block's absent and inverted qualia and Chinese nation objections, from 'Troubles with Functionalism', as challenges to functionalism.

note: dennett's functionalist account of consciousness
why: Page quotes Consciousness Explained: 'I am a sort of teleofunctionalist, perhaps the original teleofunctionalist'.

note: models are simplifications, not the thing
why: Review: her book counterbalances functionalist tendencies; computational models are abstractions and the brain is disanalogous to a computer.

note: 'what it is like' becomes the hard problem
why: Chalmers states the hard problem using Nagel (1974): there is something it is like to be a conscious organism.

note: from gap to hard problem
why: Chalmers writes there is an explanatory gap, 'a term due to Levine 1983', between the functions and experience.

note: the mill argument is cited as an early version of the hard problem
why: Pages list Leibniz among earlier thinkers with similar arguments; none says Chalmers built on the mill.

note: walking around inside the machine and finding no understanding
why: SEP names Leibniz's mill as the first of four antecedents of Searle's argument.
